title_en: Stardy Shipping Co., Ltd. v. China Shipping Development Co., Ltd. — dispute over compensation for damages from non-contact collision of vessels

full_text_en:
Studio Shipping Company Ltd. v. China Shipping Development Co., Ltd.

— Dispute over compensation for damage from non-contact collision of ships

Plaintiff: Studio Shipping Company Ltd. (STUDIO SHIPPING COMPANY LTD.). Domicile: PENTELIDES STREET, NICOSIA, CYPRUS.
Legal Representative: Philippos Philip, Director and Manager of the Company.
Agent ad litem: Chen Fayin, Attorney at Shanghai Hualian Law Firm.
Agent ad litem: Sun Yafeng, Attorney at Shanghai Donghua Law Firm.

Defendant: China Shipping Development Co., Ltd. (formerly Shanghai Haixing Shipping Co., Ltd.). Domicile: No. 168, Yuanshen Road, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Li Kelin, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Company.
Agent ad litem: Cai Cunqiang, Attorney at Shanghai Haixiang Law Firm.
Agent ad litem: Lu Min, Attorney at Shanghai Huisheng Law Firm.

The Plaintiff, Studio Shipping Company Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "Studio"), filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai Maritime Court against the Defendant, China Shipping Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "China Shipping"), for compensation for damage arising from a non-contact collision of ships.

Plaintiff's Allegations: During the navigation of the Defendant's vessel "Zhenxing" in the Huangpu River, it improperly used VHF (Very High Frequency radiotelephone) and sound signals, sailed at excessive speed, failed to give way to the vessel proceeding with the current, and abruptly altered course to occupy the fairway when approaching the Plaintiff's vessel "Gemini". These acts of the "Zhenxing" in violation of navigation regulations created a danger to the navigation of the "Gemini". Despite taking various measures, the "Gemini" managed to pass the "Zhenxing" with only a 1-meter gap between the two ships. However, the "Gemini" was ultimately pushed towards the shore by the powerful wake current from the "Zhenxing's" propeller, colliding with vessels moored at the shore and indirectly damaging dock facilities. Pursuant to the _International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972_ and the _Port Regulations of Shanghai Port_, the Defendant should bear liability for this collision incident involving the "Gemini". The Plaintiff requests the Court to order the Defendant to compensate the Plaintiff for economic losses totaling USD 931,394.50 and RMB 2,698,704.42.

Defendant's Defense: During this voyage, the "Zhenxing" was sailing behind the "Yingxiang", which was following a small boat and sailing at a slow speed. While navigating, the "Zhenxing" consistently sailed along the right side of the outbound fairway, displayed the required navigation lights, exhibited trial signals, monitored VHF as required, and promptly communicated its navigation status. When passing Buoy No. 106, although the "Zhenxing" deviated from its own fairway to avoid a small boat, it corrected its course and continued sailing safely after passing. When the "Gemini" was sighted, the "Zhenxing" used sound signals and VHF to report its navigation movements. The two vessels passed each other port-to-port safely off Berths No. 3 and 4 of Zhanghuabang, with a transverse distance of approximately 40 meters between their sterns at the time of passing. During the passing, no sound signals from the "Gemini" were heard. The time of the passing alleged by the Plaintiff coincided with the ebb tide. Based on speed calculations, the vessel meeting the "Gemini" at that time should have been the "Yingxiang", not the "Zhenxing". The "Zhenxing" only heard news of the "Gemini's" accident on VHF when it arrived near the Navy Pier. The "Zhenxing" did not experience any incidents during this voyage and certainly did not collide with any part of the "Gemini". The alleged incident involving the "Gemini" was entirely caused by its own excessive speed, misjudgment, and improper maneuvering, and is unrelated to the "Zhenxing". The Court should dismiss the Plaintiff's claims.

Basic Facts Found by the Court:

The Shanghai Maritime Court found through trial:

At about 2000 hours on November 8, 1993, the Plaintiff's vessel "Gemini" entered the Huangpu River from the quarantine anchorage outside the Wusongkou, proceeding upstream with the flood tide, engine at half ahead, speed approximately 4.4 knots. At about 2100 hours, the "Gemini's" starboard side was abeam of the Wusong Passenger Terminal. Ahead, it sighted the "Zhenxing" proceeding downstream against the current in the outbound fairway off the Jungong Road Terminal, with a distance of about 1500 meters between the two vessels. At about 2105 hours, the "Gemini" arrived off Berths No. 2 and 3 of Zhanghuabang and observed the "Zhenxing" turning to port into the inbound fairway, then making a large turn to starboard to exit. The distance between the two vessels was then about 600 meters. The "Gemini" gradually reduced its speed to dead slow (approximately 2 knots). At about 2107 hours, after the "Gemini" passed the "Zhenxing" off Berth No. 5 of Zhanghuabang, to keep clear of the vessels moored near the shore, it took measures including port ten degrees rudder, hard-a-port, and half ahead. However, the effect of the turn to port was not obvious. The "Gemini" immediately took further measures: stop engine, crash astern, and drop both anchors. At about 2110 hours, the "Gemini" successively collided with the barge "Huo 0903", the tugboats "Haigang 19" and "Haigang 6", and the vessel "Liming", all moored at Berth No. 7 of Zhanghuabang, and indirectly collided with the berth No. 7 of Zhanghuabang.

After the incident, the Master of the "Gemini" issued a "Sea Protest" on the following day, stating: At about 2107 hours, the pilot ordered stop engine; at about 2108 hours, the pilot ordered half astern and let go the starboard anchor; then full astern and let go the port anchor, followed by emergency astern. During this period, the "Gemini" collided with 2 tugboats and 1 barge, stopping engines at 2110 hours. The "Pilotage Accident Report" of the "Gemini's" pilot stated: Due to the "Zhenxing's" sudden large-angle turn into the inbound fairway, to avoid a collision, starboard ten degrees rudder was used to turn the bow to starboard. At a transverse distance of 20 meters from the moored vessels off Berth No. 5 of Zhanghuabang, the "Gemini" passed the "Zhenxing" with a distance of less than 1 meter between them. Subsequently, port ten degrees rudder and hard-a-port rudder were used to turn the bow to port. However, due to the influence of the wake current from the "Zhenxing's" propeller, the bow turned very slowly, and the use of half ahead was ineffective. When the accident became unavoidable, to minimize damage, measures of stop engine, crash astern, and dropping both anchors were taken. As a result, the midships of the "Gemini" came to rest against the "Haigang 19" moored at Berth No. 7 of Zhanghuabang.

The Defendant's vessel "Zhenxing" had departed from the Youlong Road Pier of Lixin Shipyard at 1900 hours on that day for a trial voyage downstream against the current. After passing Buoy No. 106, to avoid a small boat anchored in the middle of the fairway, the "Zhenxing" turned to port and entered the inbound fairway. After passing the small boat, it turned to starboard and proceeded towards the outbound fairway. It passed the "Gemini" at about 2107 hours.

In the "Report on the Navigation Situation of the 'Zhenxing' Trial Voyage Outbound on the Huangpu River on the Evening of November 8, 1993" submitted to the Shanghai Harbor Superintendency Administration after the incident, the Master of the "Zhenxing" stated: While sailing on the Huangpu River, the 'Zhenxing' passed abeam of Buoy No. 106 at 2121 hours and sighted a small boat about 500 meters ahead and to starboard, which had encroached upon part of the outbound fairway. The 'Zhenxing' passed close astern of the small boat and immediately turned to starboard to correct its position. At 2126 hours, the 'Zhenxing' safely passed the 'Gemini' at a distance of about 130 meters from Berths No. 3 and 4 of Zhanghuabang, with a transverse distance of about 40 meters between their sterns during the passing. During this time, no avoidance sound signals from the 'Gemini' were heard.

The Shanghai Maritime Court commissioned navigation experts from the Institute of Navigation Technology, Dalian Maritime University, to conduct an analysis of the tracks of the "Gemini" and the "Zhenxing". The appraisal report ruled out the possibility that the "Yingxiang" met the "Gemini" at 2107 hours, concluding that the vessels meeting at that time must have been the "Gemini" and the "Zhenxing", and the meeting point should have been off Berth No. 5 of Zhanghuabang. Although the appraisal report did not determine the distance between the two ships at the time of passing, it expressed doubt regarding the "Zhenxing's" Master's claim that the sterns of the two ships passed at a distance of 40 meters. The appraisal report also determined that the speed of the "Zhenxing" on some sections of the fairway was approximately 7 knots, exceeding the limit of 6 knots for upstream navigation against the current as stipulated in the _Port Regulations of Shanghai Port_, constituting excessive speed. The conclusion was: "It cannot be ruled out that the 'Zhenxing' caused the 'Gemini' to collide with the moored vessels at Berth No. 7 of Zhanghuabang."

This incident caused damage to the vessel "Gemini". The Plaintiff, Studio, incurred the following expenses: repair costs of USD 132,300; classification society survey fees of USD 3,932.65; shifting fees in Shanghai Port of USD 5,685.70. From the date of collision to the completion of repairs, 18 days and 3 hours elapsed. The "Gemini's" daily charter hire was USD 7,750. Consequently, Studio suffered operating losses totaling USD 140,468.74.

The incident also caused damage to the berth No. 7 of Zhanghuabang. After negotiation, Studio paid USD 550,000 to the Shanghai Port Zhanghuabang Stevedoring Company as compensation. It also caused damage to the vessel "Liming". After negotiation, Studio paid USD 8,041 to the owner of the "Liming" as compensation. The total losses incurred by Studio as set forth above amounted to USD 840,428.09. Damage was also caused to the barge "Huo 0903" and the tugboats "Haigang 19" and "Haigang 6", for which related litigation is pending.

The above facts are confirmed by the following evidence: the Appraisal Report; the Sea Protest of the Master of the "Gemini"; the Pilotage Accident Report of the "Gemini's" pilot; the Situation Report made to the Shanghai Harbor Superintendency Administration by the pilot of the "Yingxiang"; the Sea Protest of the barge "Huo 0903"; the Sea Protests of the tugboats "Haigang 19" and "Haigang 6"; the Navigation Situation Report by the Master of the "Zhenxing". All evidence was subject to examination in court and can serve as the basis for determining the facts of this case.

Reasoning of the Court:

The Shanghai Maritime Court held: This case involves a dispute over compensation for damage from a non-contact collision of ships. To determine whether the alleged non-contact offending vessel bears liability, it is first necessary to ascertain whether the two involved vessels actually met, the time and place of such meeting. Only then can the respective liabilities of the parties be determined.

Based on the reports of the "Gemini" and the vessels it collided with, the time of the collision between the "Gemini" and the vessels moored at Berth No. 7 of Zhanghuabang was 2110 hours. The Navigation Situation Report of the "Zhenxing's" Master stated that the "Zhenxing" met the "Gemini" at Berths No. 3 and 4 of Zhanghuabang at 2126 hours. This statement not only contradicts the undisputed fact that the "Gemini" was involved in an accident at Berth No. 7 of Zhanghuabang at 2110 hours, but also conflicts with the Defendant China Shipping's own claim that the vessel meeting the "Gemini" at 2107 hours should have been the "Yingxiang". Based on the positions of the berths at Zhanghuabang Wharf, the "Zhenxing" necessarily had to pass Berth No. 7 before reaching Berths No. 3 and 4. If the "Zhenxing" met the "Gemini" at Berths No. 3 and 4 only at 2126 hours, the "Gemini" could not have been involved in an accident at Berth No. 7, a location it would not have reached by 2110 hours. Furthermore, if the "Gemini" was still off Berths No. 3 and 4 at 2126 hours, the "Yingxiang", which was sailing ahead of the "Zhenxing", could not have met the "Gemini" off Berth No. 5 at 2107 hours. Accordingly, it can be confirmed that the vessel that met the "Gemini" off Berth No. 5 of Zhanghuabang at 2107 hours was the "Zhenxing".

Whether each vessel kept to its own fairway during the passing is key to determining fault. To resolve this key issue, the distance between the two vessels at the time of passing must first be determined. The "Gemini" claimed the distance was only 1 meter, while the "Zhenxing" claimed it was 40 meters. Although the appraisal report did not make a determination on this point, it expressed doubt about the "Zhenxing's" claim of passing at a 40-meter distance. Analyzing the measures taken by the "Gemini" after the passing, such as port ten degrees rudder and hard-a-port, if the "Gemini's" pilot had indeed observed the passing distance to be less than 1 meter, he would certainly not have immediately taken these measures, which would have caused the "Gemini" to steer closer towards the "Zhenxing's" side. Therefore, the "Gemini's" claim that the passing distance was only 1 meter is also untenable. Since the distance at the time of passing cannot be ascertained, the respective liabilities of the parties can only be analyzed and determined based on the degree of fault in navigation and maneuvering before and after the passing.

The time elapsed from the passing of the "Gemini" and the "Zhenxing" to the collision of the "Gemini" with other vessels was 3 minutes. Based on the speeds of the two vessels and the distance between Berth No. 5 and Berth No. 7 of Zhanghuabang, it can be determined that by the time the "Gemini" collided with other vessels, the "Zhenxing" had already moved more than 800 meters away from the "Gemini". After the "Gemini" passed the "Zhenxing", there was wide water ahead for it to navigate. Under these circumstances, to overcome the effect of the wake current from the "Zhenxing's" propeller, the "Gemini" should have increased speed to improve rudder effectiveness and proactively control its direction. Instead, the "Gemini" took measures such as port ten degrees rudder, hard-a-port, and half ahead. Observing that the rudder effect was not obvious, it then took measures: stop engine, crash astern, and drop both anchors. According to the principles of propeller forces, it was precisely the reversing action taken by the "Gemini" while moving ahead that caused its bow to swing to starboard. Coupled with the effect of the tidal current, the vessel's hull accelerated towards Berth No. 7, leading to the collision.

Rule 8(a) of the _International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972_ provides: "Any action taken to avoid collision shall, if the circumstances of the case admit, be positive, made in ample time and with due regard to the observance of good seamanship." Rule 8(f)(ii) provides: "A vessel which is required not to impede the passage or safe passage of another vessel when approaching other vessels so as to involve risk of collision is not relieved of this obligation and when taking action shall have full regard to the action which may be required by the Rules of this Part." Although the "Gemini" took measures to reduce speed upon sighting the "Zhenxing" occupying the inbound fairway, it failed to effectively control the vessel. After the two vessels passed, the "Gemini" failed to exercise good seamanship to proactively control its forward direction and avoid collision with other vessels. The "Gemini", owned by the Plaintiff Studio, violated the aforementioned provisions of the _International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972_. Its improper maneuvering measures were the primary cause of this collision. Studio shall bear 70% liability for this incident.

Rule 6(a) of the _International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972_ provides: "Every vessel shall at all times proceed at a safe speed so that she can take proper and effective action to avoid collision and be stopped within a distance appropriate to the prevailing circumstances and conditions." The "Zhenxing" sailed at excessive speed while navigating upstream against the current in some sections of the Huangpu River. As a result, when it sighted an anchored small boat occupying its forward fairway, it could not stop and wait for the "Gemini", which was proceeding downstream with the current, to pass first. It had to overtake the small boat, thus encroaching upon part of the inbound fairway. Although the "Zhenxing" did not directly collide with the "Gemini", it objectively created certain difficulties for the navigation of the "Gemini". The "Zhenxing", owned by the Defendant China Shipping, violated the aforementioned provisions of the _International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972_. China Shipping shall bear 30% liability for this incident.

In summary, the Shanghai Maritime Court, in accordance with Article 169(1) of the _Maritime Code of the PRC_ ("If two or more ships are in fault, each is liable in proportion to the degree of their respective faults. If the respective faults are equal in degree or the degrees of fault cannot be determined, the liability is apportioned equally."), Article 169(2) ("For the loss of the ships, the goods and other property on board, caused by the collision of ships in fault, the liabilities for such loss shall be borne in proportion as provided in the preceding paragraph. If the collision causes loss of property of a third party, the liability of each ship in fault shall not exceed the proportion it is required to bear."), and Article 170 ("If a ship, by reason of improper maneuvering or failure to comply with navigation regulations, causes damage to other ships, persons, goods or other property on board, although no collision actually takes place with such other ships, the provisions of this Chapter shall apply."), rendered its judgment on July 1, 1999:

Judgment:

1. The Defendant China Shipping shall compensate the Plaintiff Studio for vessel repair costs of USD 39,690, plus interest;
2. The Defendant China Shipping shall compensate the Plaintiff Studio for vessel operating losses of USD 42,140.62, plus interest;
3. The Defendant China Shipping shall compensate the Plaintiff Studio for vessel survey fees of USD 1,179.80, plus interest;
4. The Defendant China Shipping shall compensate the Plaintiff Studio for shifting fees of USD 1,705.71, plus interest;
5. The Defendant China Shipping shall compensate the Plaintiff Studio for losses from the Zhanghuabang Wharf of USD 165,000, plus interest;
6. The Defendant China Shipping shall compensate the Plaintiff Studio for losses concerning the vessel "Liming" of USD 2,412.30, plus interest;
7. The Plaintiff's other claims are dismissed.

Interest on the above sums shall be calculated at the USD demand deposit rate of the People's Bank of China, from the date each expense was incurred by the Plaintiff Studio until the effective date of this judgment.

The above sums shall be paid in full by the Defendant China Shipping to the Plaintiff Studio within 10 days from the effective date of this judgment.

Court acceptance fee: USD 16,280, to be borne by the Plaintiff Studio (USD 11,396) and the Defendant China Shipping (USD 4,884); Appraisal fee: RMB 36,960, to be borne by the Plaintiff Studio (RMB 25,872) and the Defendant China Shipping (RMB 11,088).

After the judgment was pronounced, both parties appealed to the Shanghai High People's Court.

Appeal of Studio: First, the first instance judgment erred in failing to find the facts that the "Zhenxing" occupied the inbound fairway at the time of passing and that the passing distance was less than 1 meter; its finding on the cause of the "Gemini's" collision with vessels moored outside the wharf was contrary to the facts; and there were significant omissions in the calculation of the "Gemini's" own losses. Second, the "Zhenxing" was solely responsible for creating the emergency situation during passing and should bear full liability. The "Gemini" was not at fault in its navigation, and assigning it 70% liability constitutes improper application of law. Studio requests the appellate court to amend the judgment and order China Shipping to bear full liability.

Appeal of China Shipping: 1. The "Zhenxing" could not have met the "Gemini" off Berth No. 5 of Zhanghuabang at 2107 hours; only the "Yingxiang" could have met the "Gemini" at that time. Studio's identification of the offending vessel is wrong. 2. The appraisal report's determination of the tidal current conditions at the time of the incident violates scientific principles and is erroneous. The appraisal conclusions lack factual basis and are founded on speculation and assumptions. 3. Based on evidence provided by the "Gemini", it actually sailed at excessive speed. The "Zhenxing" did not violate the speed limits of the _Port Regulations of Shanghai Port_ or the provisions on safe speed under the _International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972_. 4. The collision of the "Gemini" with the wharf and moored vessels was entirely caused by its own maneuvering errors. The "Zhenxing" should not bear 30% liability for this incident. The first instance judgment was based on unclear facts and insufficient evidence. China Shipping requests the appellate court to set aside the judgment and dismiss Studio's claims.

Shanghai High People's Court, upon trial, held that the facts found in the first instance were clear and the evidence was sufficient. The vessel that rendezvoused with the *Gemini* at 2107 hours on November 8, 1993, outside the fifth berth at Zhanghuabang, Shanghai Port, was the *Zhenxing*, a fact confirmed by the expert appraisal report and the testimonies of the relevant crew members. The appellant, Stardi Company, as the plaintiff, was unable to adduce evidence that the collision in this case was unavoidable, nor could it demonstrate that the measures taken to avoid the collision—hard to port, full ahead, stop, reverse, and dropping both anchors—were the only, correct, and reasonable measures available. The first instance judgment correctly found that *Gemini*'s own improper maneuvering was the primary cause of the collision. Stardi Company's appeal argument that the *Zhenxing* should bear full liability for the accident lacks a factual basis and is not sustained. The appellant Zhonghai Company's ground of appeal that the vessel that rendezvoused was not the *Zhenxing* is inconsistent with the facts. The *Zhenxing*, in order to avoid a small anchored vessel in the outbound channel, exceeded the speed limit and cut across a portion of the inbound channel ahead of time, objectively affecting the normal navigation of the *Gemini* and creating a tense situation at the time of the rendezvous, for which Zhonghai Company should bear some responsibility for the accident. The judgment rendered by the first instance court based on the facts of this case was correct in the application of law and appropriate in its ruling. Accordingly, pursuant to Article 153, paragraph 1, item (1) of the *Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China*, the Shanghai High People's Court, on December 25, 2000, hereby holds:

The appeal is dismissed and the original judgment is affirmed.

The second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 135,124 shall be borne equally by the appellants, Zhonghai Company and Stardi Company.
